trust.questionsTitle: Seven questions to ask any provider before you hire in Egypt
trust.questionsIntro: Ask these of every provider you consider. The answers tell you whether your people, and your company, are properly protected.

questions.title: Is the provider a registered Egyptian company?
questions.text: Ask for the commercial register and tax card. A foreign platform may rely on a local partner you never see.

questions.title: Who is the legal employer on the contract?
questions.text: The name on the contract carries the obligations to the employee and to the authorities.

questions.title: Is social insurance paid on the real wage?
questions.text: Declaring a lower wage saves a little today and creates arrears, penalties and unhappy employees later.

questions.title: Is the contract in Arabic and lawful under the current Labour Law?
questions.text: Contracts written for another country’s law do not protect you in Egypt.

questions.title: Who owns the work and the data?
questions.text: Check the IP assignment, the confidentiality agreement and how employee data is stored and transferred abroad.

questions.title: What happens when someone leaves?
questions.text: Ask who handles notice, settlements and disputes, and who pays if a claim reaches the labour court.

questions.title: Will you see proof every month?
questions.text: A good provider shows you the payroll register and insurance and tax evidence, not just an invoice.

meta.title: Hiring in Egypt: Guide for International and Gulf Companies
meta.description: Contracts, working hours, leave, pay, social insurance, tax and termination in Egypt.

guide.h1: Hiring in Egypt: a guide for international and Gulf companies
guide.summary: Egypt offers a deep, Arabic- and English-speaking talent pool in a time zone close to both the Gulf and Europe. Employment is governed by Labour Law No. 14 of 2025. You can hire through your own entity, or through an Employer of Record without opening one. Budget for salary plus around 18.75% employer social insurance on the insurable wage, and plan for a three-month notice period.
guide.reviewNote: Unreviewed source material. Figures, rates and legal interpretation must be checked against current official sources and approved by counsel before publication. Last reviewed: not yet reviewed.

chapters.title: Three ways to hire
chapters.text: Your own entity: full control, but months of set-up, capital and ongoing filings. Employer of Record: hire in weeks; the EOR is the legal employer, you manage the work. Freelance contracts: fast, but a full-time "freelancer" who works like an employee can be reclassified as one, with back-dated insurance and claims.

chapters.title: Employment contracts
chapters.text: Contracts must be written; the Arabic text governs. They can be fixed-term or indefinite, and copies are deposited with the Ministry of Labour. Probation is capped at three months. Salary is stated in Egyptian pounds.

chapters.title: Working hours
chapters.text: Standard 8 hours a day, 48 a week, usually Sunday to Thursday, with shorter hours in Ramadan. Overtime is paid at a legal premium, higher at night and on rest days. Remote, part-time and flexible work are recognised with the same rights.

chapters.title: Leave
chapters.text: Annual leave: 15 days in the first year, 21 days from the second, 30 days after 10 years or from age 50, 45 days for employees with disabilities. Casual leave: 7 days a year, taken from annual leave. Maternity: 4 months, up to three times. Paternity: one paid day at birth, up to three times. Official public holidays are set each year.

chapters.title: Pay and minimum wage
chapters.text: The private-sector minimum wage is EGP 7,000 a month (since March 2025); a private-sector change depends on the National Wages Council. Employees are entitled to an annual increase of at least 3% of their insurance wage.

chapters.title: Social insurance
chapters.text: Employer 18.75% and employee 11% of the insurable wage, which is capped at EGP 16,700 a month in 2026. Registration starts on the first day of work.

chapters.title: Income tax on salaries
chapters.text: Progressive rates from 0% to 27.5%, after an annual personal exemption of EGP 20,000. Higher earners may lose the benefit of the lower bands. The employer withholds and pays monthly.

chapters.title: Notice and termination
chapters.text: Notice is three months for indefinite contracts. Dismissal must rest on a lawful reason and a documented process. Dismissal during pregnancy or maternity leave is prohibited. Specialised labour courts have operated since October 2025.

chapters.title: Foreign employees
chapters.text: Each needs an annual work permit from the Ministry of Labour, and foreigners are generally limited to 10% of the workforce.

chapters.title: Employee data
chapters.text: The Personal Data Protection Law (No. 151 of 2020) applies. Transferring employee data abroad, including to your headquarters, needs a lawful basis and may need a permit.

chapters.title: What it really costs
chapters.text: Gross salary + employer social insurance + medical insurance (if offered) + workspace and equipment + your provider’s fee. Ask AVERA for a costed proposal for your roles.
